brief: Maths Standard Year 11 start (root request, 19 November 2026), methods of brief 243
purpose: Research route inputs for Claude, not a canonical route or teaching approval
syllabus: Mathematics Standard 11-12 (2024), Year 11 (one course common to Standard 1 and Standard 2)
identifierPolicy: Exact CMS codenames; official sourceHtml preserves mathematical layout. Year 11 is one course shared by Standard 1 and Standard 2, so standard2ActionIds and standard1ActionIds both repeat syllabusActionIds (kept for the same schema as the Year 12 files); each syllabusActions item carries the course 'Year 11 (common to Standard 1 and Standard 2)'.

officialEvidence.source: NSW Curriculum Year 11 Formulas and equations and Linear relationships pages, as recorded in the crosswalk (read 18 November 2026)

siteSource.note: Paths are repo paths at this commit, read from the read-only local clone C:/Users/kygs/teaching-app-fix at the same commit (not modified). SHA256 values recomputed from the clone on 19 November 2026 and match the crosswalk inventory. All twelve Year 11 lessons and year12/ratios-and-rates/lesson01 use data-step-id sections and label worked examples we-1 to we-4. f05, f06 and f07 have no site lesson (root ruling 3).

recommendations: Run f01 to f08, then l01 to l07, in outline order; the Year 11 course is shared by Standard 1 and Standard 2, so every video serves both. f01 is the first video of the whole Standard course: it opens cold on a concrete case with no title card. l07 hands to math-s11-e01 (Earning money).

Pace flags (gentler Standard pace): f03 and f04 are at risk (suggested splits f03a and f03b; f04a and f04b, sharing the outline number); f02, f07, l02 and l06 to watch; l07 may run short. The rest fit 6 to 9 minutes.

Year 12 dependencies checked against the Year 12 Standard packs and designs: f01 (substitution, the power key: a01, a05, a06, i01, i02), f02 (word problems: a03, i09, r03), f03 (unknown underneath and y = ax^2 + c: t01, a13, i01, a09), f04 (speed = distance ÷ time with unit changes: r04, r10, r12, f04), f08 and l05 (cells, =, *, fill down, no absolute references: a04b, i13), l01 to l03 (m and c, rise over run, steeper is faster, negative gradient as a steady fall: a01, a08, b04, i09, r12), l04 (interpolation between the data, extrapolation beyond it, the two-part limitation: a07, a11, b07), l06 and l07 (y = kx through the origin: a12).

Root rulings 3 and 4: f05, f06 and f07 teach from the syllabus alone; BAC is framed around road safety (zero BAC for learner and P-plate drivers in NSW; the formula is an estimate, never a guide to how much is safe to drink); medication doses use invented, labelled medicines with 'your doctor or pharmacist sets real doses'. Sources read 19 November 2026: nsw.gov.au 'Alcohol limits, drugs and medicines' (L, P1, P2: zero; full licence: under 0.05; 'It's impossible for you to estimate your own BAC'); health.gov.au standard drinks guide (10 g of pure alcohol). Codex re-verifies both and the dose formulas against the 2024 reference sheet.

Site findings: MS-77 to MS-83 appended to docs/production/claude-pm/site-corrections-maths-standard.md, section 12 (a reasoning-check explanation that does not give the wrong answer, a 'stopping distance' definition that is the braking distance, a solving rule that says 'last' for 'first', muddled rearranging and spreadsheet sentences, gaps for y = ax^2 + c and graphing applications, y = mx + b against the syllabus's y = mx + c). MS-01 (k for kilograms) still applies to l06.

Kit needs: docs/production/claude-pm/checks/maths-standard-kit-needs-s11-f-l.md. The main new parts are SpreadsheetGrid (already requested by math-s12-a04b, not yet built), a StoppingDistanceStrip, a FormulaSlots card for substitution and a ConversionGraph mode.
covers: math-s11-f01 to math-s11-f08 and math-s11-l01 to math-s11-l07 (Year 11 Formulas and equations and Linear relationships, common to Standard 1 and Standard 2)

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do we substitute values into a formula and trust the answer?

syllabusActions.text: Substitute numbers into linear and non-linear algebraic expressions, equations and formulas
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Substitute numbers into linear and non-linear algebraic expressions, equations and formulas

syllabusActions.text: Evaluate the subject of a formula, given the value of other pronumerals in the formula
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Evaluate the subject of a formula, given the value of other pronumerals in the formula

syllabusActions.text: Apply given formulas to solve problems in a variety of contexts
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Apply given formulas to solve problems in a variety of contexts

entryKnowledge.text: Order of operations, including powers and brackets; operations with negative numbers.
Algebraic notation: 3x means 3 × x; x^2 means x × x; x/2 means x ÷ 2.
Area and perimeter of rectangles and circles; a scientific calculator's power and π keys.

entries.startBoundary: First video of the whole Year 11 Standard course: opens cold on a concrete case (the site's delivery quote, $8 booking plus $1.50 a kilometre, for a 12 km trip), with no title card. No prior video is assumed.
entries.stopBoundary: A formula is one rule that works for many cases; name what each letter stands for (with units); substitute with brackets, then evaluate in the correct order; substitute a negative value in brackets so a power applies to the whole number; use the calculator's power key for non-linear formulas (x^2, a power such as 1.05^3); state the answer as a sentence with units and check it is sensible. Includes one 'which first move?' note from lesson08 (need an output: substitute). Solving for an input is f02; rearranging is f03; spreadsheets are f08.
entries.recommendation: First video: cold open, no title card. Keep the site's exact numbers. Must give Year 12 the substitution habits it assumes (a01 check a point; a05, a06, i02 power key; i01 formula use). Claude chooses final splits and length.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do we turn a word problem into an equation, solve it and check it makes sense?

syllabusActions.text: Represent a word problem as a linear equation, solve the equation and interpret the solution in the context of the problem
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Represent a word problem as a linear equation, solve the equation and interpret the solution in the context of the problem

entryKnowledge.text: ci7f303375 and cib2f9cd13: substituting values; a formula's letters stand for quantities with units.
Solving one-step and two-step linear equations with inverse operations (recalled here, not taught from scratch).

entries.startBoundary: f01 found an output from known inputs (12 km gives $26). Now the total is known and an input is missing: the same delivery rule, but the bill is $41 (or the site's cinema hook, 5 + 12t = 41).
entries.stopBoundary: Four steps: define the unknown with units ('Let n be the number of texts'); write the equation from the words (fixed charge + rate × unknown = total, including a falling balance such as 125 − 9w = 53); solve with inverse operations, keeping both sides balanced (undo the outside operation first); check by substitution and interpret in context, including rounding a non-whole answer the way the situation needs (up for a target, down for a budget) and rejecting impossible answers. Brackets equations appear once as an option. Rearranging a formula is f03; simultaneous equations are math-s12-a01 to a03.
entries.recommendation: Pace flag: watch. Solving is Stage 5 and is recalled, not taught from scratch; if Claude wants to teach the balance method fully, split into f02a (solving and checking) and f02b (word problems and interpretation). Must deliver what math-s12-a03, i09 and r03 assume.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do we change the subject of a formula, including y = ax^2 + c?

syllabusActions.text: Change the subject of linear and non-linear formulas limited to quadratics of the form y = ax^2 + c to solve problems and make decisions about solutions in the context of the problem
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Change the subject of linear and non-linear formulas limited to quadratics of the form y=ax2+c to solve problems and make decisions about solutions in the context of the problem
syllabusActions.siteGap: Partial in practice (the crosswalk records covered). lesson04 rearranges linear formulas only (d = st, C = 2πr, A = bh); no lesson rearranges y = ax^2 + c, takes a square root or rejects a negative root in context (MS-81). Root ruling 3 for the missing part.

entryKnowledge.text: ci2acef85d: inverse operations, keeping both sides balanced.
Substitution and a scientific calculator.
Squares and square roots; a positive number has two square roots.

entries.startBoundary: f02 solved for a number. If the same formula is used many times for a different letter, rearrange once instead (the site's hook: d = st, but we know d and t and need s).
entries.stopBoundary: The subject is the letter on its own; rearranging uses the same inverse operations as f02 but keeps letters; divide by the whole multiplier (2π, not 2); when the wanted letter is underneath (s = d/t, solve for t; y = k/x, solve for x), multiply up first, then divide; check a rearrangement with simple numbers; two-step linear rearrangements (C = 8 + 1.5k for k); y = ax^2 + c: subtract c, divide by a, then take the square root, writing ± and keeping only the root that makes sense in context (a length or time cannot be negative); rearrange first, then substitute. Quadratic graphs are math-s12-a09.
entries.recommendation: Pace flag: at risk. Suggested split: f03a (linear rearranging, including the unknown underneath) and f03b (y = ax^2 + c, the square root and rejecting the negative root). The y = ax^2 + c part is a site gap (root ruling 3). Must deliver what math-s12-t01, a13, i01 and a09 assume.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do speed, time and stopping distance connect, and why does speed matter so much?

syllabusActions.text: Calculate distance, speed and time (with change of units of measurement as required) and stopping distances of vehicles using speed = distance/time and stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Calculate distance, speed and time (with change of units of measurement as required) and stopping distances of vehicles using speed=distancetime and stopping distance=reaction distance+braking distance
syllabusActions.siteGap: Partial. year11/formulas-and-equations/lesson07 teaches only the supplied quadratic model D = 0.01v^2 + 0.3v, and its key-terms card defines stopping distance as the braking distance (MS-78). Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance and the km/h to m/s change are not taught; speed = distance/time with unit changes appears in year12/ratios-and-rates/lesson01 (used by math-s12-r10). Root ruling 3: teach the missing part from the syllabus.

entryKnowledge.text: cib54d5e23: d = st rearranged as s = d/t and t = d/s.
Substitution, including a squared term.
Time units: 60 minutes in an hour, 60 seconds in a minute; metres and kilometres.

entries.startBoundary: f03 ended with d = st in its three forms. A car's speedometer reads km/h, but a driver's reaction happens in seconds and metres: the units must match before a formula can be used.
entries.stopBoundary: speed = distance/time and its two rearrangements; converting minutes to hours (15 min = 0.25 h, never 0.15) and km/h to m/s (÷ 3.6) and back (× 3.6); stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance; reaction distance = speed in m/s × reaction time in s; braking distance read from a table or a supplied formula; why stopping distance grows faster than speed (the braking part grows with the square of speed: the site's D = 0.01v^2 + 0.3v, whose 0.3v is the reaction distance for a reaction time of 1.08 s); road-safety meaning (wet roads, tiredness and alcohol lengthen it; this sets up f05). Average speed over a multi-leg trip, rates in other units and distance-time graphs are math-s12-r10 and r12.
entries.recommendation: Pace flag: at risk. Suggested split: f04a (speed, distance, time with unit changes) and f04b (stopping distance = reaction + braking). Stopping distance as a sum is a site gap (ruling 3). Do not reuse year12 rates lesson01 we-2 (270 km in 3 h 15 min): math-s12-r10's design uses it. Example reaction times and braking distances are labelled examples; Codex checks them against Transport for NSW guidance.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do the BAC formulas estimate blood alcohol from drinks, hours and body weight?

syllabusActions.text: Apply the formulas BAC_male = (10N - 7.5H)/(6.8M) and BAC_female = (10N - 7.5H)/(5.5M) to calculate and interpret blood alcohol content (BAC) based on drink consumption and body weight, where N is the number of standard drinks consumed, H is the number of hours of drinking and M is the person’s weight in kilograms
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Apply the formulas BACmale=10N - 7.5H6.8M and BACfemale=10N - 7.5H5.5M to calculate and interpret blood alcohol content (BAC) based on drink consumption and body weight, where N is the number of standard drinks consumed, H is the number of hours of drinking and M is the person’s weight in kilograms
syllabusActions.siteGap: Missing. No lesson teaches the BAC formulas (lesson05 names them in a notice). Root rulings 3 and 4: teach from the syllabus, framed around road safety; P-platers must have zero BAC; the formula is an estimate, never a guide to how much is safe to drink.

entryKnowledge.text: ci61d581aa: reaction distance grows with reaction time; anything that slows reactions lengthens stopping distance.
Substituting into a formula with a fraction and brackets; rounding at the end.
Decimals to three places; order of operations with a numerator and denominator.

entries.startBoundary: f04 ended on reaction time: alcohol slows reactions. The law measures alcohol as blood alcohol content, and NSW learner and P-plate drivers must have zero.
entries.stopBoundary: What BAC measures (grams of alcohol per 100 mL of blood: 0.05 means 0.05 g in every 100 mL); the NSW limits in one line (zero for learner, P1 and P2 drivers; under 0.05 for full licence holders); a standard drink (10 g of pure alcohol); the two syllabus formulas, with N, H and M named; substituting with the numerator and denominator worked separately, rounding to three decimal places at the end; interpreting a result (any BAC above zero means a P-plater must not drive; a result under 0.05 is an estimate, not a safe number; a negative result means the model estimates zero); why the female formula gives a higher BAC for the same N, H and M (5.5 < 6.8). Examples are invented adults. Time to zero and the limitations are f06.
entries.recommendation: Syllabus-only video (root ruling 3). Root ruling 4 binds: road-safety framing, P-platers zero BAC, the formula is an estimate and never a guide to how much is safe to drink. No people, no drinking scenes; drinks shown as a count, not glamorised glasses. Sources: nsw.gov.au 'Alcohol limits, drugs and medicines' (read 19 Nov 2026); health.gov.au standard drinks guide.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How long until BAC returns to zero, and why is any BAC estimate only rough?

syllabusActions.text: Apply the formula Time = BAC/0.015 to determine the number of hours required for a person to stop consuming alcohol in order to reach zero BAC
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Apply the formula Time=BAC0.015 to determine the number of hours required for a person to stop consuming alcohol in order to reach zero BAC
syllabusActions.siteGap: Missing. No lesson teaches Time = BAC/0.015. Root rulings 3 and 4.

syllabusActions.text: Identify and explain the limitations of methods used to estimate BAC
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Identify and explain the limitations of methods used to estimate BAC
syllabusActions.siteGap: Missing. No lesson discusses the limitations of BAC estimates. Root rulings 3 and 4.

entryKnowledge.text: ci9f40765a: an estimated BAC from the formula; zero for learner and P-plate drivers.
Rearranging and dividing; converting a decimal number of hours to hours and minutes (math-s11-f04's time units).

entries.startBoundary: f05's invented driver had an estimated BAC of about 0.032. A P-plater needs zero: how long until the model says zero?
entries.stopBoundary: Time = BAC/0.015 (the body removes about 0.015 of BAC each hour in this model); converting decimal hours to hours and minutes and rounding up (waiting less is not enough); using the unrounded BAC from f05 where possible; the next-morning case (a high BAC late at night can still be above zero the next morning); limitations: the formulas assume a fixed rate and average bodies, while real BAC depends on food, body build, health, medication, drink size and how fast drinks were had; drinks poured at home are often bigger than a standard drink; only a breath or blood test measures BAC; NSW Government: 'It's impossible for you to estimate your own BAC'. The only safe plan for a P-plater is no alcohol before driving.
entries.recommendation: Syllabus-only video (ruling 3); ruling 4 binds. Keep a limitation as two parts (the assumption, why it fails), the pattern math-s12-a07 uses. Codex confirms the quoted NSW sentence and the date read.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do Fried's, Young's and Clark's formulas scale a medicine dose for a child?

syllabusActions.text: Calculate the required medication dosages for children and adults given age or weight, using Fried’s, Young’s and Clark’s formula as appropriate
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Calculate the required medication dosages for children and adults given age or weight, using Fried’s, Young’s and Clark’s formula as appropriate
syllabusActions.siteGap: Missing. No lesson teaches Fried's, Young's or Clark's formula. Root rulings 3 and 4: invented, clearly labelled medicines and doses; 'your doctor or pharmacist sets real doses' on screen and in narration.

entryKnowledge.text: Substituting into a fraction formula; rounding at the end.
Months and years (12 months in a year).
Mass in kilograms and milligrams.

entries.startBoundary: f06 showed that a formula can only estimate what a body does. Medicine doses are another case where a formula gives a starting estimate and a professional decides.
entries.stopBoundary: Why a child's dose is scaled down from an adult dose; Fried's formula (age in months, for infants), Young's formula (age in years, for children), Clark's formula (weight in kg); choosing the formula from the information given and the age; comparing two formulas for one child and saying why they differ (age and weight are different proxies); an adult dose from a per-kilogram rate (mg per kg × mass); stating the dose with units and sensible rounding. Every medicine and dose is invented and labelled; 'your doctor or pharmacist sets real doses' on screen and in narration. Liquid volumes (mL from mg) are optional.
entries.recommendation: Syllabus-only video (ruling 3); ruling 4 binds. The formula forms follow the NESA Standard reference sheet; Codex confirms them, and the age ranges for each, against the current 2024 reference sheet before narration. Pace flag: watch (three formulas plus a per-kg adult case).

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How does a spreadsheet apply one formula to a whole table of cases?

syllabusActions.text: Use a spreadsheet to perform calculations involving formulas
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Use a spreadsheet to perform calculations involving formulas

syllabusActions.text: Apply given formulas to solve problems in a variety of contexts
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Apply given formulas to solve problems in a variety of contexts

entryKnowledge.text: Substitution into a formula, with order of operations.
Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance (the capstone table).
Reading a table with rows and columns.

entries.startBoundary: The strand has used one formula at a time. A spreadsheet uses one formula for many cases at once: the site's canteen order (=B2*C2+D2).
entries.stopBoundary: A spreadsheet as a grid of cells named by column and row; a formula starts with = and uses cell references in place of letters; * for times, / for divide, ^ for a power; reading =B2*C2+D2 as T = qc + f; filling down, where the references change row by row (=B2*C2 becomes =B3*C3); changing one input updates every result; keeping units consistent in a column; one strand capstone: a column of speeds and a filled-down stopping-distance formula, so the table shows how fast stopping distance grows. Absolute references are not taught (consistent with math-s12-a04b). Linear models in a spreadsheet are l05.
entries.recommendation: Must deliver what math-s12-a04b assumes (cells, =, *, fill down with relative references). New kit part SpreadsheetGrid is needed (not yet built). Closes the Formulas and equations strand.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: What do the gradient and y-intercept tell us, from a graph or an equation?

syllabusActions.text: Determine the y-intercept and gradient of a straight line given in graphical form
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Determine the y-intercept and gradient of a straight line given in graphical form

syllabusActions.text: Determine the y-intercept and gradient from the equation of a straight line
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Determine the y-intercept and gradient from the equation of a straight line

entryKnowledge.text: Tables of values produced by a formula.
The Cartesian plane, plotting points (x, y), reading scales; gradient as rise over run and y = mx + c met in Stage 5 (recalled, not assumed fluent).

entries.startBoundary: f08's spreadsheet made tables. Plot one table and the points line up: a straight line has two numbers that describe it completely.
entries.stopBoundary: The y-intercept as the value where the line crosses the vertical axis (the output when x = 0); the gradient as rise over run between two clear points, with its sign (up: positive, down: negative, flat: zero); steeper means a bigger rate; gradient = change in output ÷ change in input, never the reverse; gradient with units in context (dollars per week, litres per minute); reading m and c straight from y = mx + c, including y = 12 − 3x (m = −3, c = 12) and C = 12 + 5h. Writing the equation and drawing the line are l02; building a model from words is l03.
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's exact numbers. Use y = mx + c (the syllabus letters), not the site's y = mx + b (MS-82). Must deliver what math-s12-a01, a08, b04 and r12 assume.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do we write y = mx + c and draw the line, by hand and with technology?

syllabusActions.text: Determine the equation of a straight line of the form y = mx + c where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Determine the equation of a straight line of the form y=mx+c where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept

syllabusActions.text: Construct a straight-line graph, with and without using graphing applications
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Construct a straight-line graph, with and without using graphing applications
syllabusActions.siteGap: Covered by hand (tables to points in linear-relationships/lesson01); no lesson uses a graphing application (MS-81). The 'with graphing applications' half is original teaching.

entryKnowledge.text: ci94641a48 and cic0a28004: gradient and y-intercept from a graph or an equation.
Substituting x values to make a table.

entries.startBoundary: l01 read m and c from a line. Now go the other way: given m and c (or a graph, or a table), write the equation and draw the line.
entries.stopBoundary: Writing y = mx + c from a gradient and an intercept, from a graph (read c, count m) and from a table (c is the output at x = 0; m is the constant difference for steps of 1); checking a table is linear by equal differences for equal steps (lesson01); drawing a line by hand from a table of at least three points with a ruler, or by plotting c and stepping the gradient; drawing the same line in a graphing application and checking a point; every point on the line makes the equation true. Writing a model from words is l03; two lines crossing is math-s12-a01.
entries.recommendation: The graphing-application half is original teaching (site gap). HSC Standard calculators do not graph; the app is a classroom tool. Must deliver math-s12-a01's start boundary (a line drawn from y = mx + c and a short table). Pace flag: watch.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How does a linear model describe a real situation, and what do its gradient and intercept mean?

syllabusActions.text: Model linear relationships and interpret the features of those relationships in a variety of contexts, noting that the y-intercept is the vertical intercept and the gradient is the rate of change
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Model linear relationships and interpret the features of those relationships in a variety of contexts, noting that the y-intercept is the vertical intercept and the gradient is the rate of change

entryKnowledge.text: ciafd3b572: writing y = mx + c.
ci2acef85d: solving a linear equation in context.

entries.startBoundary: l02 wrote equations for lines. Real situations come with words, not m and c: the site's bike hire, $12 before riding plus $5 an hour.
entries.stopBoundary: Building a linear model from words or a table: the starting value is the vertical intercept (the amount when the input is zero), the rate is the gradient (the change for each one unit of input); define both variables with units; negative gradients as a steady fall (V = 200 − 15h); interpreting the intercept and gradient in a sentence with units; using the model to find an output (substitute) or an input (solve, f02); changing one feature (a price rise changes the gradient only). When predictions can be trusted is l04.
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's exact numbers. Must deliver what math-s12-a03, a04a, i01 and i09 assume (intercept as starting value, gradient as rate, a negative gradient as a steady fall).

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: When can we trust a prediction from a linear model?

syllabusActions.text: Interpolate and extrapolate from a linear model in a practical context
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Interpolate and extrapolate from a linear model in a practical context
syllabusActions.siteGap: Missing. No Year 11 lesson teaches interpolation or extrapolation from a linear model (section 2 of the site corrections). Root ruling 3.

syllabusActions.text: Identify and describe the limitations of a linear model in a practical context
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Identify and describe the limitations of a linear model in a practical context
syllabusActions.siteGap: Partial. formulas-and-equations/lesson05 checks differences before assuming a linear pattern; limitations of a linear model in context are not taught. Root ruling 3 for the missing part.

entryKnowledge.text: cib2d6c0df: a linear model with its intercept and gradient in context.
Solving a linear equation for an input.

entries.startBoundary: l03's models gave a cost for any number of hours. Can we trust the answer for 30 hours, or for minus 2?
entries.stopBoundary: A model is built from values over a range; interpolation is predicting inside that range (fairly safe); extrapolation is predicting outside it (less reliable, more so the further out, but not automatically wrong); nonsense answers (a negative amount of fuel, a cost for an impossible time) are warning signs; limitations of a linear model: it assumes the same rate for ever, so caps, new prices, running out or physical limits break it; values below zero; stating a limitation in two parts (the assumption, why it fails here); the valid input range in a sentence. Lines of best fit for data are math-s12-b04 and b07; exponential limitations are math-s12-a07.
entries.recommendation: Interpolation and extrapolation are a site gap (ruling 3); limitations are partial. Use the words math-s12-b07 and a07 assume ('interpolation = between the data', 'extrapolation = beyond it', the two-part limitation). a07 uses a fare cap; do not repeat it here.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How does a spreadsheet build and test a linear model?

syllabusActions.text: Use a spreadsheet to model a linear relationship in a variety of contexts
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Use a spreadsheet to model a linear relationship in a variety of contexts
syllabusActions.siteGap: Partial. Spreadsheet formulas are taught generally in formulas-and-equations/lesson06; no lesson builds a linear model in a spreadsheet. Root ruling 3 for the missing part.

entryKnowledge.text: ciffbbbd58: spreadsheet formulas, cell references and fill down.
cib2d6c0df: a linear model's intercept and gradient.
ci4777471a and ci1b3cf962: interpolation, extrapolation and a valid range.

entries.startBoundary: l04 ended with a model and its valid range. A spreadsheet can lay out every case in that range at once.
entries.stopBoundary: Building a linear model in a spreadsheet: an input column filled with a step, an output column with a formula such as =150+18*A2 filled down; checking the output column has a constant difference equal to the gradient; reading the intercept in the row where the input is 0; a line chart from the two columns; finding when the output first reaches a target (bracket between two rows, refine the step, round in context); changing the rate or the fixed amount in the formula and watching every row and the chart update; comparing to the algebra answer. Break-even with two columns is math-s12-a04b.
entries.recommendation: Partial site coverage (ruling 3 for the missing part). Must deliver what math-s12-a04b and i13 assume (math-s12-i13's pack calls l05 the first spreadsheet video; f08 is first). Do not teach break-even (a04b).

entryKnowledge.text: cib2d6c0df: a linear model with a starting value and a rate.
ci94641a48: gradient from a graph.

entries.startBoundary: Every l03 model had a starting amount. Some have none: apples at $4 a kilogram with no fixed fee (the site's hook). Zero kilograms costs zero.
entries.stopBoundary: Direct variation y = kx: no fixed amount, so the line passes through the origin; k is the constant of variation, the gradient and the rate (output per one unit of input); y/x = k for every point with x ≠ 0; doubling x doubles y; recognising direct variation from a description (no fee, starts at zero, 'per') and from a table (constant ratio, and y = 0 at x = 0 if that row is shown); not every straight line is direct variation (y = 5x + 12); finding k from one pair and using y = kx to find other values in both directions. Graphing and reading y = kx is l07.
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's numbers but use m (not k) for kilograms (MS-01). Must deliver what math-s12-a12 assumes (y = kx is a straight line through the origin; k constant). Pace flag: watch (four points).

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do we graph y = kx and use the graph to solve problems?

syllabusActions.text: Graph and analyse equations of the form y = kx to solve problems in a variety of contexts
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Graph and analyse equations of the form y=kx to solve problems in a variety of contexts

entryKnowledge.text: cie0224c11, ci6f88d684, cic7837e3f and ci04c5dcb2: y = kx, k from one pair.
ci5ff71229: drawing a straight line by hand and with a graphing application.

entries.startBoundary: l06 found k from one pair. Two points fix a line, and the origin is always one of them, so one more point is enough to draw a direct variation graph.
entries.stopBoundary: Graphing y = kx from the origin and one calculated point (and a check point); a larger k gives a steeper line; reading values off the graph in both directions (across to the line, down to the axis), including a conversion graph (currency); comparing two direct variations on one set of axes; using the graph to answer a practical question and checking with the equation; reading k back from a graph (rise over run from the origin). Closes the Linear relationships strand.
entries.recommendation: Pace flag: may run short (about 5 minutes is acceptable, as root accepted near 5,000-character videos). Exchange rates are labelled example rates that change daily (ruling 5 pattern). Final frame hands to math-s11-e01 (Earning money; another author's strand).
